sets.title: Travel writing, empire and gender
sets.contentHtml:
Mode of transportation affects the travel experience and thus can produce new types of travel writing and perhaps even new “identities.” Modes of transportation determine the types and duration of social encounters; affect the organization and passage of space and time; . . . and also affect perception and knowledge—how and what the traveler comes to know and write about. The completion of the first U.S. transcontinental highway during the 1920s . . . for example, inaugurated a new genre of travel literature about the United States—the automotive or road narrative. Such narratives highlight the experiences of mostly male protagonists “discovering themselves” on their journeys, emphasizing the independence of road travel and the value of rural folk traditions.

Travel writing’s relationship to empire building— as a type of “colonialist discourse”—has drawn the most attention from academicians. Close connections have been observed between European (and American) political, economic, and administrative goals for the colonies and their manifestations in the cultural practice of writing travel books. Travel writers’ descriptions of foreign places have been analyzed as attempts to validate, promote, or challenge the ideologies and practices of colonial or imperial domination and expansion. Mary Louise Pratt’s study of the genres and conventions of 18th- and 19th-century exploration narratives about South America and Africa (e.g., the “monarch of all I survey” trope) offered ways of thinking about travel writing as embedded within relations of power between metropole and periphery, as did Edward Said’s theories of representation and cultural imperialism. Particularly Said’s book, Orientalism, helped scholars understand ways in which representations of people in travel texts were intimately bound up with notions of self, in this case, that the Occident defined itself through essentialist, ethnocentric, and racist representations of the Orient. Said’s work became a model for demonstrating cultural forms of imperialism in travel texts, showing how the political, economic, or administrative fact of dominance relies on legitimating discourses such as those articulated through travel writing.

Feminist geographers’ studies of travel writing challenge the masculinist history of geography by questioning who and what are relevant subjects of geographic study and, indeed, what counts as geographic knowledge itself. Such questions are worked through ideological constructs that posit men as explorers and women as travelers—or, conversely, men as travelers and women as tied to the home. Studies of Victorian women who were professional travel writers, tourists, wives of colonial administrators, and other (mostly) elite women who wrote narratives about their experiences abroad during the 19th century have been particularly revealing. From a “liberal” feminist perspective, travel presented one means toward female liberation for middle- and upper-class Victorian women. Many studies from the 1970s onward demonstrated the ways in which women’s gendered identities were negotiated differently “at home” than they were “away,” thereby showing women’s self-development through travel. The more recent poststructural turn in studies of Victorian travel writing has focused attention on women’s diverse and fragmented identities as they narrated their travel experiences, emphasizing women’s sense of themselves as women in new locations, but only as they worked through their ties to nation, class, whiteness, and colonial and imperial power structures.

sets.title: Bregman’s Humankind
sets.contentHtml:
Although one of the most contested concepts in political philosophy, human nature is something on which most people seem to agree. By and large, according to Rutger Bregman in his new book Humankind, we have a rather pessimistic view – not of ourselves exactly, but of everyone else. We see other people as selfish, untrustworthy and dangerous and therefore we behave towards them with defensiveness and suspicion. This was how the 17th-century philosopher Thomas Hobbes conceived our natural state to be, believing that all that stood between us and violent anarchy was a strong state and firm leadership.

But in following Hobbes, argues Bregman, we ensure that the negative view we have of human nature is reflected back at us. He instead puts his faith in Jean-Jacques Rousseau, the 18th-century French thinker, who famously declared that man was born free and it was civilisation – with its coercive powers, social classes and restrictive laws – that put him in chains.

Hobbes and Rousseau are seen as the two poles of the human nature argument and it’s no surprise that Bregman strongly sides with the Frenchman. He takes Rousseau’s intuition and paints a picture of a prelapsarian idyll in which, for the better part of 300,000 years, Homo sapiens lived a fulfilling life in harmony with nature . . . Then we discovered agriculture and for the next 10,000 years it was all property, war, greed and injustice. . . .

It was abandoning our nomadic lifestyle and then domesticating animals, says Bregman, that brought about infectious diseases such as measles, smallpox, tuberculosis, syphilis, malaria, cholera and plague. This may be true, but what Bregman never really seems to get to grips with is that pathogens were not the only things that grew with agriculture – so did the number of humans. It’s one thing to maintain friendly relations and a property-less mode of living when you’re 30 or 40 hunter-gatherers following the food. But life becomes a great deal more complex and knowledge far more extensive when there are settlements of many thousands.

“Civilisation has become synonymous with peace and progress and wilderness with war and decline,” writes Bregman. “In reality, for most of human existence, it was the other way around.” Whereas traditional history depicts the collapse of civilisations as “dark ages” in which everything gets worse, modern scholars, he claims, see them more as a reprieve, in which the enslaved gain their freedom and culture flourishes. Like much else in this book, the truth is probably somewhere between the two stated positions.

In any case, the fear of civilisational collapse, Bregman believes, is unfounded. It’s the result of what the Dutch biologist Frans de Waal calls “veneer theory” – the idea that just below the surface, our bestial nature is waiting to break out. There’s a great deal of reassuring human decency to be taken from this bold and thought-provoking book and a wealth of evidence in support of the contention that the sense of who we are as a species has been deleteriously distorted. But it seems equally misleading to offer the false choice of Rousseau and Hobbes when, clearly, humanity encompasses both.

sets.title: Human contact as a luxury good
sets.contentHtml:
[There is] a curious new reality: Human contact is becoming a luxury good. As more screens appear in the lives of the poor, screens are disappearing from the lives of the rich. The richer you are, the more you spend to be off-screen. . . .

The joy — at least at first — of the internet revolution was its democratic nature. Facebook is the same Facebook whether you are rich or poor. Gmail is the same Gmail. And it’s all free. There is something mass market and unappealing about that. And as studies show that time on these advertisement-support platforms is unhealthy, it all starts to seem déclassé, like drinking soda or smoking cigarettes, which wealthy people do less than poor people. The wealthy can afford to opt out of having their data and their attention sold as a product. The poor and middle class don’t have the same kind of resources to make that happen.

Screen exposure starts young. And children who spent more than two hours a day looking at a screen got lower scores on thinking and language tests, according to early results of a landmark study on brain development of more than 11,000 children that the National Institutes of Health is supporting. Most disturbingly, the study is finding that the brains of children who spend a lot of time on screens are different. For some kids, there is premature thinning of their cerebral cortex. In adults, one study found an association between screen time and depression. . . .

Tech companies worked hard to get public schools to buy into programs that required schools to have one laptop per student, arguing that it would better prepare children for their screen-based future. But this idea isn’t how the people who actually build the screen-based future raise their own children. In Silicon Valley, time on screens is increasingly seen as unhealthy. Here, the popular elementary school is the local Waldorf School, which promises a back-to-nature, nearly screen-free education. So as wealthy kids are growing up with less screen time, poor kids are growing up with more. How comfortable someone is with human engagement could become a new class marker.

Human contact is, of course, not exactly like organic food. But with screen time, there has been a concerted effort on the part of Silicon Valley behemoths to confuse the public. The poor and the middle class are told that screens are good and important for them and their children. There are fleets of psychologists and neuroscientists on staff at big tech companies working to hook eyes and minds to the screen as fast as possible and for as long as possible. And so human contact is rare. . . .

There is a small movement to pass a “right to disconnect” bill, which would allow workers to turn their phones off, but for now a worker can be punished for going offline and not being available. There is also the reality that in our culture of increasing isolation, in which so many of the traditional gathering places and social structures have disappeared, screens are filling a crucial void.

sets.title: Explaining the economic crisis
sets.contentHtml:
I’ve been following the economic crisis for more than two years now. I began working on the subject as part of the background to a novel, and soon realized that I had stumbled across the most interesting story I’ve ever found. While I was beginning to work on it, the British bank Northern Rock blew up, and it became clear that, as I wrote at the time, “If our laws are not extended to control the new kinds of super-powerful, super-complex, and potentially super-risky investment vehicles, they will one day cause a financial disaster of global-systemic proportions.” . . . I was both right and too late, because all the groundwork for the crisis had already been done—though the sluggishness of the world’s governments, in not preparing for the great unraveling of autumn 2008, was then and still is stupefying. But this is the first reason why I wrote this book: because what’s happened is extraordinarily interesting. It is an absolutely amazing story, full of human interest and drama, one whose byways of mathematics, economics, and psychology are both central to the story of the last decades and mysteriously unknown to the general public. We have heard a lot about “the two cultures” of science and the arts—we heard a particularly large amount about it in 2009, because it was the fiftieth anniversary of the speech during which C. P. Snow first used the phrase. But I’m not sure the idea of a huge gap between science and the arts is as true as it was half a century ago—it’s certainly true, for instance, that a general reader who wants to pick up an education in the fundamentals of science will find it easier than ever before. It seems to me that there is a much bigger gap between the world of finance and that of the general public and that there is a need to narrow that gap, if the financial industry is not to be a kind of priesthood, administering to its own mysteries and feared and resented by the rest of us. Many bright, literate people have no idea about all sorts of economic basics, of a type that financial insiders take as elementary facts of how the world works. I am an outsider to finance and economics, and my hope is that I can talk across that gulf.

My need to understand is the same as yours, whoever you are. That’s one of the strangest ironies of this story: after decades in which the ideology of the Western world was personally and economically individualistic, we’ve suddenly been hit by a crisis which shows in the starkest terms that whether we like it or not—and there are large parts of it that you would have to be crazy to like—we’re all in this together. The aftermath of the crisis is going to dominate the economics and politics of our societies for at least a decade to come and perhaps longer.

questions.stemHtml: According to the passage, Said’s book, “Orientalism”:

options.textHtml: explained the difference between the representation of people and the actual fact.
illustrated how narrow minded and racist westerners were.
argued that cultural imperialism was more significant than colonial domination.
demonstrated how cultural imperialism was used to justify colonial domination

questions.solutionHtml:
D. Said’s work showed that ‘the political, economic, or administrative fact of dominance relies on legitimating discourses’ such as travel writing, i.e. cultural imperialism (how the Orient was represented) served to justify colonial domination.

A is not the point: the book is about how representations were tied to the West’s idea of itself, not about measuring representation against ‘actual fact’.

B goes too far: the passage says the Occident used racist representations to define itself; it does not say the book set out to show how narrow-minded westerners were.

C invents a ranking: nothing says cultural imperialism was ‘more significant’ than colonial domination; the two are linked, not compared.

questions.stemHtml: From the passage, it can be inferred that scholars argue that Victorian women experienced self-development through their travels because:

options.textHtml: their identity was redefined when they were away from home.
they were on a quest to discover their diverse identities.
they were from the progressive middle- and upper-classes of society.
they developed a feminist perspective of the world

questions.solutionHtml:
A. The third paragraph links self-development directly to identity: studies showed women’s gendered identities ‘were negotiated differently “at home” than they were “away,” thereby showing women’s self-development through travel’. Being away redefined who they were.

B reverses cause and effect: the ‘diverse and fragmented identities’ are what poststructural scholars focus on, not a quest the women set out on.

C describes their class, which is background, not the reason scholars give for self-development.

D confuses the scholars’ (liberal feminist) perspective with the women’s own; the passage does not say the travellers developed a feminist outlook.

questions.stemHtml: From the passage, we can infer that feminist scholars’ understanding of the experiences of Victorian women travellers is influenced by all of the following EXCEPT scholars':

options.textHtml: awareness of gender issues in Victorian society
awareness of the ways in which identity is formed
perspective that they bring to their research
knowledge of class tensions in Victorian society

questions.solutionHtml:
D is the exception. Class appears only as one of the ‘ties’ women worked through (nation, class, whiteness) and in the description of travellers as middle- and upper-class. Nothing suggests scholars draw on knowledge of class tensions in Victorian society.

A is present: feminist geographers question the masculinist history of geography and gendered constructs (men as explorers, women as travellers).

B is present: scholars study how gendered identities were ‘negotiated’ at home and away, and the poststructural focus on ‘diverse and fragmented identities’.

C is present: the ‘liberal’ feminist perspective and the later poststructural turn show that the scholars’ own lens shapes their reading.

questions.stemHtml: American travel literature of the 1920s:

options.textHtml: developed the male protagonists’ desire for independence.
showed participation in local traditions.
presented travellers’ discovery of their identity as different from others.
celebrated the freedom that travel gives.

questions.solutionHtml:
D. The road narratives of the 1920s emphasised ‘the independence of road travel’, i.e. they celebrated the freedom that travel gives.

A says the literature ‘developed’ the protagonists’ desire for independence; the passage only says the narratives emphasised the independence of road travel, not that they created a desire in the characters.

B is a stretch: the narratives valued ‘rural folk traditions’, which is not the same as showing travellers taking part in them.

C adds a comparison: protagonists were ‘discovering themselves’, but nothing says their identity was shown as different from others’.

questions.stemHtml: From the passage, we can infer that travel writing is most similar to:

options.textHtml: historical fiction
political journalism
feminist writing
autobiographical writing

questions.solutionHtml:
D. Throughout the passage travel writing is the traveller’s own account of his or her journey: protagonists ‘discovering themselves’, women who ‘wrote narratives about their experiences abroad’ and ‘narrated their travel experiences’. A first-person account of one’s own life and experiences is autobiographical writing.

A fails: travel writing is not presented as fiction set in the past.

B fails: it can carry political ideology (colonialist discourse), but it is not reporting on politics.

C fails: feminist scholars study travel writing; the writing itself is not feminist writing.

questions.stemHtml: The author has differing views from Bregman regarding:

options.textHtml: a civilised society being coercive and unjust.
a property-less mode of living being socially harmonious.
the role of agriculture in the advancement of knowledge.
the role of pathogens in the spread of infectious diseases.

questions.solutionHtml:
A. Bregman sides with Rousseau: civilisation, with ‘its coercive powers, social classes and restrictive laws’, put man in chains, and after agriculture ‘it was all property, war, greed and injustice’. The author pushes back: the truth is ‘somewhere between the two stated positions’ and offering the choice of Rousseau or Hobbes is ‘misleading’ because ‘humanity encompasses both’. So the author does not share Bregman’s view of civilised society as coercive and unjust.

B is something the author concedes: ‘It’s one thing to maintain friendly relations and a property-less mode of living when you’re 30 or 40 hunter-gatherers’.

C is the author’s own point about knowledge growing in large settlements; Bregman is said to have overlooked it, not to have argued the opposite.

D is accepted: ‘This may be true’ is the author’s response to Bregman’s claim about agriculture and disease.

questions.stemHtml: According to the author, the main reason why Bregman contrasts life in pre-agricultural societies with agricultural societies is to:

options.textHtml: make the argument that an environmentally conscious lifestyle is a more harmonious way of living.
bolster his argument that people are basically decent, but progress as we know it can make them selfish.
advocate the promotion of less complex societies as a basis for greater security and prosperity.
highlight the enormous impact that settled farming had on population growth.

questions.solutionHtml:
B. Bregman’s thesis is that human nature is decent and that the pessimistic Hobbesian view is wrong. The contrast (300,000 years of harmony vs. 10,000 years of ‘property, war, greed and injustice’ after agriculture) supports Rousseau’s idea that people are born good and civilisation corrupts them.

A picks up ‘harmony with nature’ but turns it into an environmental argument the book does not make.

C overstates: Bregman is not advocating a return to simpler societies; he is making a claim about human nature.

D is the author’s counterpoint (population grew with agriculture), not Bregman’s reason for the contrast.

questions.stemHtml: According to the passage, the “collapse of civilisations” is viewed by Bregman as:

options.textHtml: a time that enables changes in societies and cultures.
a sign of regression in society’s trajectory.
a temporary phase which can be rectified by social action.
resulting from a breakdown in the veneer of human nature.

questions.solutionHtml:
A. Bregman cites modern scholars who see such collapses ‘more as a reprieve, in which the enslaved gain their freedom and culture flourishes’, i.e. a time that allows societies and cultures to change.

B is the traditional ‘dark ages’ view that Bregman rejects.

C invents ‘social action’ to rectify the phase; Bregman does not treat collapse as something to fix.

D is veneer theory, which Bregman calls the source of an unfounded fear.

questions.stemHtml: None of the following views is expressed in the passage EXCEPT that:

options.textHtml: Bregman agrees with Hobbes that firm leadership is needed to ensure property rights and regulate strife.
Hobbes and Rousseau disagreed on the fundamental nature of humans, but both believed in the need for a strong state.
the author of the review believes in the veneer theory of human nature.
most people agree with Hobbes’ pessimistic view of human nature as being intrinsically untrustworthy and selfish.

questions.solutionHtml:
We need the one view that IS expressed. D. The opening says most people agree on human nature and hold a pessimistic view of others as ‘selfish, untrustworthy and dangerous’, which ‘was how … Thomas Hobbes conceived our natural state to be’.

A is false: Bregman sides with Rousseau, not Hobbes.

B is false: only Hobbes is said to believe in a strong state; Rousseau blamed civilisation’s coercive powers.

C is false: the reviewer says humanity encompasses both natures; nowhere does he endorse veneer theory.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements about the negative effects of screen time is the author least likely to endorse?

options.textHtml: It can cause depression in viewers.
It is designed to be addictive.
It increases human contact as it fills an isolation void.
It is shown to have adverse effects on young children’s learning.

questions.solutionHtml:
C. The author does say screens are ‘filling a crucial void’ in an isolated culture, but never that screen time increases human contact; the whole argument is that screens make human contact rare. C is also not a negative effect at all, so it is the statement the author would not endorse.

A is supported: ‘one study found an association between screen time and depression’.

B is supported: psychologists and neuroscientists work ‘to hook eyes and minds to the screen’.

D is supported: children with over two hours a day ‘got lower scores on thinking and language tests’.

questions.stemHtml: The author is least likely to agree with the view that the increase in screen-time is fuelled by the fact that:

options.textHtml: screens provide social contact in an increasingly isolating world.
with falling costs, people are streaming more content on their devices.
some workers face punitive action if they are not online.
there is a growth in computer-based teaching in public schools

questions.solutionHtml:
B. Falling costs and streaming are never mentioned. The services discussed are already free; the drivers named are design, marketing to schools, work pressure and isolation.

A is in the last paragraph: screens are ‘filling a crucial void’ in a culture of isolation.

C is there too: ‘a worker can be punished for going offline’.

D matches tech companies pushing ‘one laptop per student’ programmes in public schools.

questions.stemHtml: The author claims that Silicon Valley tech companies have tried to “confuse the public” by:

options.textHtml: promoting screen time in public schools while opting for a screen-free education for their own children.
developing new work-efficiency programmes while lobbying for the “right to disconnect” bill.
concealing the findings of psychologists and neuroscientists on screen-time use from the public.
pushing for greater privacy while working with advertisement-support platforms to mine data.

questions.solutionHtml:
A. The companies sold one-laptop-per-student programmes to public schools and tell the poor and middle class that screens are ‘good and important for them and their children’, while their own children attend a ‘nearly screen-free’ Waldorf School. Saying one thing while doing another is the confusion.

B is not in the passage: tech companies are not said to lobby for the ‘right to disconnect’ bill.

C twists the detail: the psychologists work to hook users; nothing is said about hiding their findings.

D is not stated: privacy is mentioned only as something the wealthy can buy.

questions.stemHtml: The statement “The richer you are, the more you spend to be off-screen” is supported by which other line from the passage?

options.textHtml: “How comfortable someone is with human engagement could become a new class marker.”
“. . . screens are filling a crucial void.”
“. . . studies show that time on these advertisement-support platforms is unhealthy . . .”
“Gmail is the same Gmail. And it’s all free.”

questions.solutionHtml:
A. The claim links wealth to staying off screens. ‘How comfortable someone is with human engagement could become a new class marker’ says the same thing: time spent with people rather than screens tracks class.

B is about screens filling a gap left by isolation, which has nothing to do with the rich paying to avoid screens.

C explains why screens seem déclassé, but it is about health, not about spending money to opt out.

D stresses that the services are the same for everyone and free, the opposite of a class difference.

questions.stemHtml: Which one of the following best captures the main argument of the last paragraph of the passage?

options.textHtml: Whoever you are, you would be crazy to think that there is no crisis.
The aftermath of the crisis will strengthen the central ideology of individualism in the Western world.
The ideology of individualism must be set aside in order to deal with the crisis.
In the decades to come, other ideologies will emerge in the aftermath of the crisis.

questions.solutionHtml:
C. The paragraph’s ‘irony’ is that after decades of individualistic ideology, the crisis shows ‘we’re all in this together’. The implied argument is that the crisis has to be faced collectively, i.e. the individualistic outlook has to give way.

A misuses the word ‘crazy’, which refers to liking parts of the crisis, not to denying it exists.

B is the opposite: the crisis undercuts individualism.

D predicts new ideologies; the paragraph only says the aftermath will dominate economics and politics.

questions.stemHtml: Which one of the following, if true, would be an accurate inference from the first sentence of the passage?

options.textHtml: The author’s preoccupation with the economic crisis is not less than two years old.
The economic crisis outlasted the author’s preoccupation with it.
The author has witnessed many economic crises by travelling a lot for two years.
The author is preoccupied with the economic crisis because he is being followed.

questions.solutionHtml:
A. ‘I’ve been following the economic crisis for more than two years now’ means his preoccupation is at least two years old, i.e. not less than two years old.

B cannot be inferred: he is still following it, so nothing says the crisis outlasted his interest.

C misreads ‘following’ as travelling and adds ‘many crises’.

D reads ‘following’ literally, as if someone were following him.

questions.stemHtml: Which one of the following, if false, could be seen as supporting the author’s claims?

options.textHtml: Most people are yet to gain any real understanding of the workings of the financial world.
The global economic crisis lasted for more than two years.
The huge gap between science and the arts has steadily narrowed over time.
The economic crisis was not a failure of collective action to rectify economic problems.

questions.solutionHtml:
Negate each option and see which negation backs the author. D: ‘The crisis was not a failure of collective action’; if false, the crisis was a failure of collective action. That fits the author’s complaint about ‘the sluggishness of the world’s governments’ and his point that ‘we’re all in this together’.

A negated says most people do understand finance, which contradicts his claim of a big gap between finance and the public.

B negated (the crisis lasted two years or less) does nothing for him; he expects its aftermath to last a decade or more.

C negated (the science–arts gap has not narrowed) contradicts his view that the gap is smaller than it was.

questions.stemHtml: All of the following, if true, could be seen as supporting the arguments in the passage, EXCEPT:

options.textHtml: The difficulty with understanding financial matters is that they have become so arcane.
Economic crises could be averted by changing prevailing ideologies and beliefs.
The story of the economic crisis is also one about international relations, global financial security, and mass psychology.
The failure of economic systems does not necessarily mean the failure of their ideologies.

questions.solutionHtml:
D is the exception. The passage treats the crisis as exposing the individualistic ideology (‘we’re all in this together’). Saying a system’s failure need not mean its ideology failed works against that.

A supports the claim that finance is like a ‘priesthood, administering to its own mysteries’, far from the general public.

B fits the point that the crisis challenges decades of individualistic ideology; a change of beliefs is the lesson drawn.

C fits the ‘absolutely amazing story’ whose byways of mathematics, economics and psychology matter, with global (‘global-systemic’) consequences.

questions.stemHtml: According to the passage, the author is likely to be supportive of which one of the following programmes?

options.textHtml: An educational curriculum that promotes economic research.
Economic policies that are more sensitively calibrated to the fluctuations of the market.
An educational curriculum that promotes developing financial literacy in the masses.
The complete nationalisation of all financial institutions.

questions.solutionHtml:
C. The author wants to narrow the gap between finance and the general public, noting that ‘many bright, literate people have no idea about all sorts of economic basics’. Financial literacy for the masses is exactly that.

A is about research, which serves specialists, not the general reader he wants to reach.

B is a policy fix for markets; the passage is about public understanding.

D is an extreme step the passage never suggests.

questions.stemHtml:
Five sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a meaningful and coherent short paragraph. Identify the odd one out. Choose its number as your answer and key it in.

1. Machine learning models are prone to learning human-like biases from the training data that feeds these algorithms.

2. Hate speech detection is part of the on-going effort against oppressive and abusive language on social media.

3. The current automatic detection models miss out on something vital: context.

4. It uses complex algorithms to flag racist or violent speech faster and better than human beings alone.

5. For instance, algorithms struggle to determine if group identifiers like "gay" or "black" are used in offensive or prejudiced ways because they're trained on imbalanced datasets with unusually high rates of hate speech.
questions.solutionHtml:
Chain 2-4-1-5. 2 introduces hate speech detection; 4 (‘It uses complex algorithms…’) explains how it works; 1 gives the catch: these models learn biases from training data; 5 (‘For instance…’) illustrates that bias, ending on ‘trained on imbalanced datasets’, which echoes 1’s ‘training data’.

Sentence 3 blames a different flaw, missing context. The paragraph’s problem is biased training data, so 3 is the odd one out: 3.

questions.stemHtml:
Identify the most appropriate summary for the paragraph.

Aesthetic political representation urges us to realize that ‘the representative has autonomy with regard to the people represented’ but autonomy then is not an excuse to abandon one’s responsibility. Aesthetic autonomy requires cultivation of ‘disinterestedness’ on the part of actors which is not indifference. To have disinterestedness, that is, to have comportment towards the beautiful that is devoid of all ulterior references to use – requires a kind of aesthetic commitment; it is the liberation of ourselves for the release of what has proper worth only in itself.

options.textHtml: Aesthetic political representation advocates autonomy for the representatives drawing from disinterestedness, which itself is different from indifference.
Aesthetic political representation advocates autonomy for the representatives manifested through disinterestedness which itself is different from indifference.
Disinterestedness is different from indifference as the former means a non-subjective evaluation of things which is what constitutes aesthetic political representation.
Disinterestedness, as distinct from indifference, is the basis of political representation.

questions.solutionHtml:
Key points: (i) aesthetic political representation gives representatives autonomy, (ii) that autonomy requires cultivating disinterestedness, (iii) disinterestedness is not indifference.

A keeps all three, and ‘drawing from disinterestedness’ captures that the autonomy rests on (requires) disinterestedness.

B is very close but says the autonomy is ‘manifested through’ disinterestedness, i.e. disinterestedness becomes how autonomy shows itself. The paragraph says autonomy needs disinterestedness as a precondition, so ‘drawing from’ is the better fit.

C says disinterestedness constitutes aesthetic political representation and drops autonomy.

D drops ‘aesthetic’ and autonomy and turns disinterestedness into the basis of all political representation.

questions.stemHtml:
Five sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a meaningful and coherent short paragraph. Identify the odd one out. Choose its number as your answer and key it in.

1. The logic of displaying one’s inner qualities through outward appearance was based on a distinction between being a woman and being feminine.

2. 'Appearance' became a signifier of conduct - to look was to be and conformity to the feminine ideal was measured by how well women could use the tools of the fashion and beauty industries.

3. The makeover-centric media sets out subtly and not-so-subtly, ‘good’ and ‘bad’ ways to be a woman, layering these over inequalities of race and class.

4. The denigration of working-class women and women of colour often centres on their perceived failure to embody feminine beauty.

5. ‘Woman’ was considered a biological category, but femininity was a ‘process’ by which women became specific kinds of women.
questions.solutionHtml:
Chain 1-5-2-4. 1 sets up the distinction between being a woman and being feminine; 5 defines both sides (woman = biological, femininity = a process); 2 says appearance became the measure of femininity, judged by how well women used fashion and beauty tools; 4 gives the consequence: working-class women and women of colour are denigrated for ‘failure to embody feminine beauty’.

Sentence 3 brings in a new subject, ‘makeover-centric media’, and what it does today. The other four are about the idea of femininity and how women are judged by it, so 3 is the odd one out: 3.

questions.stemHtml:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given in this question, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order for the sentences and key in this sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Each one personified a different aspect of good fortune.

2. The others were versions of popular Buddhist gods, Hindu gods and Daoist gods.

3. Seven popular Japanese deities, the Shichi Fukujin, were considered to bring good luck and happiness.

4. Although they were included in the Shinto pantheon, only two of them, Daikoku and Ebisu, were indigenous Japanese gods.
questions.solutionHtml:
3 introduces the seven deities and is the opener. 1 (‘Each one…’) describes them. 4 says only two were native Japanese gods, and 2 (‘The others…’) can only follow that, covering the remaining five.

4-2 is a fixed pair, giving 3142.

questions.stemHtml:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given in this question, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order for the sentences and key in this sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. Complex computational elements of the CNS are organized according to a “nested” hierarchic criterion; the organization is not permanent and can change dynamically from moment to moment as they carry out a computational task.

2. Echolocation in bats exemplifies adaptation produced by natural selection; a function not produced by natural selection for its current use is exaptation -- feathers might have originally arisen in the context of selection for insulation.

3. From a structural standpoint, consistent with exaptation, the living organism is organized as a complex of “Russian Matryoshka Dolls” -- smaller structures are contained within larger ones in multiple layers.

4. The exaptation concept, and the Russian-doll organization concept of living beings deduced from studies on evolution of the various apparatuses in mammals, can be applied for the most complex human organ: the central nervous system (CNS).
questions.solutionHtml:
2 must open: it defines adaptation and exaptation, the term the other sentences rely on.

4 comes next and sets out the paragraph’s thesis. The exaptation concept and the Russian-doll organization concept, both taken from studies of how mammalian body systems evolved, can be applied to the CNS. 4 calls the Russian-doll idea an existing concept from the literature (‘deduced from studies on evolution’), so it does not need an earlier sentence to introduce it.

3 then explains the second concept that 4 announced: ‘from a structural standpoint’, organisms are built like Matryoshka dolls, with smaller structures nested inside larger ones in several layers. This prepares for 1, which shows the same picture in the CNS: its computational elements are organized in a ‘nested’ hierarchy, and that hierarchy can change from moment to moment. 3 → 1 is the tightest link in the paragraph (nesting in organisms → nesting in the CNS), and 1 makes a good closing sentence.

Order: 2431. 2341 is the closest alternative. It also reads smoothly, because 3 picks up ‘consistent with exaptation’ right after 2. But it separates 3 from 1, so the general idea of nesting no longer leads straight into the CNS example. It also leaves the thesis (4) in the middle instead of at the start.

questions.stemHtml:
Identify the most appropriate summary for the paragraph.

The dominant hypotheses in modern science believe that language evolved to allow humans to exchange factual information about the physical world. But an alternative view is that language evolved, in modern humans at least, to facilitate social bonding. It increased our ancestors’ chances of survival by enabling them to hunt more successfully or to cooperate more extensively. Language meant that things could be explained and that plans and past experiences could be shared efficiently.

options.textHtml: Most believe that language originated from a need to articulate facts, but others think it emerged from the need to promote social cohesion and cooperation, thus enabling human survival.
From the belief that humans invented language to process factual information, scholars now think that language was the outcome of the need to ensure social cohesion and thus human survival.
Since its origin, language has been continuously evolving to higher forms, from being used to identify objects to ensuring human survival by enabling our ancestors to bond and cooperate.
Experts are challenging the narrow view of the origin of language, as being merely used to describe facts and label objects, to being necessary to promote more complex interactions among humans.

questions.solutionHtml:
The paragraph contrasts the dominant view (language for exchanging facts) with an alternative (language for social bonding and cooperation, which aided survival).

A keeps both views and their relation: most hold the first, others the second.

B says scholars have moved from one belief to the other; the paragraph says the factual view is still dominant.

C invents language ‘evolving to higher forms’ over time.

D calls the dominant view narrow and adds ‘label objects’; it also misses that it is still the dominant view.

questions.stemHtml:
Identify the most appropriate summary for the paragraph.

Brown et al. (2001) suggest that ‘metabolic theory may provide a conceptual foundation for much of ecology just as genetic theory provides a foundation for much of evolutionary biology’. One of the successes of genetic theory is the diversity of theoretical approaches and models that have been developed and applied. A Web of Science (v. 5.9. Thomson Reuters) search on genetic* + theor* + evol* identifies more than 12000 publications between 2005 and 2012. Considering only the 10 most-cited papers within this 12000 publication set, genetic theory can be seen to focus on genome dynamics, phylogenetic inference, game theory and the regulation of gene expression. There is no one fundamental genetic equation, but rather a wide array of genetic models, ranging from simple to complex, with differing inputs and outputs, and divergent areas of application, loosely connected to each other through the shared conceptual foundation of heritable variation.

options.textHtml: Genetic theory has a wide range of theoretical approaches and applications and Metabolic theory must have the same in the field of ecology.
Genetic theory has evolved to spawn a wide range of theoretical models and applications but Metabolic theory need not evolve in a similar manner in the field of ecology.
Genetic theory has a wide range of theoretical approaches and application and is foundational to evolutionary biology and Metabolic theory has the potential to do the same for ecology.
Genetic theory provides an example of how a range of theoretical approaches and applications can make a theory successful.

questions.solutionHtml:
The paragraph: metabolic theory may do for ecology what genetic theory does for evolutionary biology; genetic theory is foundational and succeeds through a wide range of approaches and models.

C keeps both halves: genetic theory’s range and its foundational role, and metabolic theory’s potential to do the same.

A says metabolic theory ‘must’ have the same; the paragraph only says it ‘may’.

B adds a claim that metabolic theory ‘need not’ evolve similarly, which is not there.

D leaves out metabolic theory and ecology, the point the paragraph opens with.

questions.stemHtml:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given in this question, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order for the sentences and key in this sequence of four numbers as your answer.

1. It advocated a conservative approach to antitrust enforcement that espouses faith in efficient markets and voiced suspicion regarding the merits of judicial intervention to correct anticompetitive practices.

2. Many industries have consistently gained market share, the lion’s share - without any official concern; the most successful technology companies have grown into veritable titans, on the premise that they advance ‘public interest’.

3. That the new anticompetitive risks posed by tech giants like Google, Facebook, and Amazon, necessitate new legal solutions could be attributed to the dearth of enforcement actions against monopolies and the few cases challenging mergers in the USA.

4. The criterion of ‘consumer welfare standard’ and the principle that antitrust law should serve consumer interests and that it should protect competition rather than individual competitors was an antitrust law introduced by, and named after, the 'Chicago school'.
questions.solutionHtml:
4 introduces the Chicago school and its consumer welfare standard. 1 begins with ‘It advocated…’, and ‘It’ needs that antecedent, so 4-1 is a fixed pair.

2 shows the result of that hands-off approach: industries gained market share ‘without any official concern’ and tech firms became titans. 3 concludes: the new risks from these tech giants need new legal solutions because of the lack of enforcement.

Order: 4123.
